analysis:
The supplied changes are documentation only: a new changelog fragment (changelog.d/gemma-byte-fallback-flush.md, lines 1-6) and a paragraph added to docs/architecture/inference.md (head lines ~1561-1569). Neither changes executable code, so no new attack surface or control regression is visible. The prose describes a provider-side tokenizer bridge change in LocalTokenizerLoader.swift: LocalTokenizerBridge.decode now releases a trailing run of <0xHH> byte-fallback tokens. That source file was not supplied, so the described behavior is unverified.

Security-relevant claims for the next pass to check against the code:
1. Decoded text and logprobs gain entries for byte tokens. Per the changelog, logprobs text and bytes become U+FFFD or an ASCII character instead of empty. This should not leak anything beyond the already-authorized consumer response (A-001), and it travels the same E2E-encrypted path (T-008).
2. A stop string that a trailing run completes now matches one token sooner, so completion_tokens can fall by one. The docs treat this as a billing and usage nuance. No billing-integrity impact is evident, but the coordinator's token accounting is outside this scope.
3. The changelog states that token IDs, cache keys and sampling are unchanged. If true, the prefix-cache threat T-041 (HMAC-keyed names, scope folding) is unaffected. That claim cannot be verified without the code.
4. The docs claim DetokenizerV2 holds back partial U+FFFD runs. Memory-bounds or DoS implications of that buffering for adversarial byte-token sequences (T-010, T-029) are unverified.

No finding qualifies. Because the actual implementation is outside the supplied evidence, the code-level behavior is a coverage limit rather than evidence of safety. I flag that for a reviewer who sees the Swift change.
